terms.gloss: quarrel, dispute; also go to law
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.37.2: Hirtium cum Quīnctiō ācerrimē lītigāsse (Lewis & Short)
Ter. And. 2.3.15: cedo, quid jūrgābit tēcum? (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Rep. 4.8: jūrgāre igitur lēx putat inter sē vīcīnōs, nōn lītigāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The milder word: Cicero says neighbours jūrgant, they do not lītigant.

terms.gloss: brawl, come to blows or hard words
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.240: cum esset cum eō dē amīculā rixātus (Lewis & Short)
Hor. Ep. 1.18.15: dē lānā caprīnā (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Quid istuc est? quīcum lītigās, Olympiō? — Cum eādem quā tū semper.
phrases.english: What’s this? Who are you quarrelling with, Olympio? — With the same woman you always are.

phrases.latin: Quid est? quā dē rē lītigātis nunc inter vōs?
phrases.english: What is it? What are you two quarrelling about now?

sources: Lewis & Short: litigo · Lewis & Short: jurgo · Lewis & Short: rixor
